closingStory: What I like most about The Quiet Hour is that it was never meant to be a perfectly controlled studio production. It started with me asking my suitemate if he wanted to take some pictures, turned into an outfit discussion, and eventually became a late-night experiment with three Godox flashes, a new camera, a new flash, two outfits, multiple locations, and two photographers taking turns trying things. I got to experiment with flash power, shutter speed, ISO, aperture, light placement, and the relationship between artificial light and nighttime ambient light. More importantly, I got to see how much you can create with a relatively simple setup when you are willing to experiment. The shoot gave me a chance to try a category of photography I had been wanting to explore, while also becoming one of my first real creative projects with the A7 IV. It was a fun way to end the semester: go outside at night, bring way too much lighting equipment, take what feels like a million photographs, move around until something works, and figure things out as we go. And honestly, that's probably why I enjoyed it so much.

sections.text: I had been wanting to do a shoot with my suitemate for a while. I always thought he would make a really good model, and I knew he had already worked with photographers and modeled for them a few times. So one night, while he was heading out, I finally asked him, "Hey, do you wanna do a photoshoot with me?"

He was immediately down. We started talking about what he could wear right there, and he showed me a few different outfits. I ended up really liking two of them. The first was a blue hoodie with light blue jeans and a white T-shirt underneath, paired with his blue-and-white Jordans and a Club Mocchi-Mocchi Super Mario Bob-Omb Mega 15 inch Plush. The second was almost the complete opposite: a black sweatshirt with red flames, black pants with matching red flames, and black-and-red Jordans.
At that point, though, the shoot was still completely up in the air. We had talked about the outfits, but there wasn't really a date or plan yet.
Then my Spring 2026 semester finals ended. Everyone was finally free, I was going back home soon for the summer, and I thought, you know what? This is the perfect way to end the semester.

I wanted to do something creative before leaving, so I asked him if we should finally make the shoot happen. I decided I wanted to do it at night around Old Main. I had just bought a Godox iT32 flash, and I really wanted to experiment with it. The idea in my head was a nighttime street-style shoot where I could use flash creatively instead of relying entirely on whatever ambient light happened to be around.

When we got to Old Main, my photographer friend came through in a big way. He had brought an octagonal softbox with a studio flash, as well as another Godox on-camera flash. Since all three flashes were from Godox, we were able to put together a DIY three-light setup. The studio flash inside the octagonal softbox became the key light, positioned roughly 45 degrees from the subject. I placed my own detachable flash low on the ground toward the left side of the subject. The main light was coming from the right, so this gave the left side of his body a very subtle highlight instead of letting it disappear completely into shadow. The other on-camera flash was placed on a light stand behind the model and became the hair/rim light. It helped separate him from the background and outline his body against the darker environment. I had seen three-light setups like this online before, but actually putting one together myself was a completely different experience. It was one thing to understand where a key light, fill light, and hair light should go; it was another to physically move the lights around, look at what they were doing, and adjust everything until the photograph looked right. One of my favorite photographs from the entire shoot is portrait-thequiethour-4. You can actually see the flash positioned behind him shining directly into the lens while he's looking away from the key light and smiling. I don't even know exactly how to describe why I like it so much—it just has this really interesting feeling to it. The combination of the flare, his expression, the darkness around him, and the lighting makes the photograph feel different from a conventional portrait.

My friend and I took turns shooting. I would photograph him for a while, choosing my own location and poses, and then we'd switch so my friend could shoot his interpretation. After that we'd move somewhere else and repeat the process.
It felt like we could keep doing it forever.

Having three lights meant there were so many combinations to experiment with. I could change the angle, move the lights, change the subject's position, try different poses, and then adjust the shutter speed, ISO, aperture, and flash power to get the look I wanted.
It became less like simply taking portraits and more like having a little photography laboratory in the middle of the night.

It was also a very DIY experience, which is something I really enjoyed. We didn't have some elaborate professional studio setup. We had the equipment we had brought with us, a few flashes, a softbox, some stands, and a location we were able to work with. Somehow, that was enough to create something that felt much more elaborate than what we had started with.

We eventually moved on to the second outfit. The black-and-red outfit had a completely different energy from the blue one, and I immediately thought about the architecture around Durham Hall. The brick exterior felt like it would work really well with the black-and-red clothing, so we moved there and continued shooting.
The process was pretty much the same. We experimented with different positions, poses, lighting arrangements, and angles, and my friend got his own set of photographs as well.
When I eventually posted the photographs on Instagram, they got a really good response, which made the whole thing even more rewarding.

editingStory: A few days later, I went through and edited the photographs. The editing itself was relatively straightforward. I wasn't trying to completely transform the photographs in post; I mainly wanted to preserve the different moods created during the shoot and let the lighting and environment do most of the work.
conclusion:
Looking back, this shoot ended up being a lot more than just a photoshoot with my suitemate. It was one of my first creative shoots with the Sony A7 IV, which made it particularly meaningful to me. Technically, the graduation shoot I did earlier was the first shoot I ever did with the camera, but that was client work, so in my head, The Quiet Hour was really my first proper creative experiment with it.

It was also my first time really getting to experiment with my new Godox flash, one of my first attempts at building a proper multi-light setup myself, and another opportunity to explore the kind of creative street-style photography I had been wanting to try. So, yeah, maybe I should call this shoot New Beginnings.

New camera. New flash. New lighting setups. New experiments.
